query: dotnet api in docker can't connect to postgres localhost

threads.title: Node.js app in Docker: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432

question.body:
My Express app connects to Postgres fine when I run it with `node index.js`. When I build an image and run it, I get:

```
Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432
    at TCPConnectWrap.afterConnect [as oncomplete] (net.js:1141:16)
```

Postgres is running on my machine, not in a container. My pool config:

```js
const pool = new Pool({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  user: 'app',
  database: 'shop'
});
```

I run the container with `docker run -p 3000:3000 shop-api`. Why can't it see Postgres?

comments.author: jvdberg
comments.text: Which OS? The answer is different on Linux and on Docker Desktop.

answers.body:
Inside the container, `localhost` is the container itself, not your machine. Each container gets its own network namespace, so `127.0.0.1` points at the container's own loopback interface. Nothing listens on 5432 there, so the connection is refused.

You have two options:

**1. Run Postgres in a container too** and put both on one network. With Compose, the service name becomes the host name:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      PGHOST: db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
```

**2. Keep Postgres on the host** and point the app at the host instead of `localhost`. On Docker Desktop (Mac and Windows) the name `host.docker.internal` resolves to the host.

**EDIT:** on Linux, `host.docker.internal` is not there by default. See the comments.

comments.author: ilya.p
comments.text: On Linux, add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` to `docker run`, or `extra_hosts` with the same value in Compose.

comments.author: rkhan
comments.text: Also check that Postgres on the host listens on more than 127.0.0.1. `listen_addresses` in postgresql.conf, and a matching line in pg_hba.conf. Took me a day.

answers.body:
Running the container with `--network host` fixed it for me:

```
docker run --network host shop-api
```

Now `localhost` works.

comments.author: tsoren
comments.text: This works on Linux because the container shares the host's network stack. It also turns off network isolation and makes `-p` meaningless. Fine for a quick test, not for anything you deploy.

comments.author: nl_dev
comments.text: Did not work for me on Docker Desktop for Mac.

answers.body:
You need to expose the Postgres port in your Dockerfile:

```
EXPOSE 5432
```

Then rebuild.

comments.author: tsoren
comments.text: `EXPOSE` is documentation. It does not publish or open anything. And Postgres is not in this container, so it is the wrong container anyway.

answers.body: Restarting Docker Desktop fixed it for me.

comments.author: jvdberg
comments.text: It probably worked because something else changed at the same time. Restarting does not change what localhost means.

threads.title: docker-compose: Flask can't connect to MySQL service, but it works with docker run

question.body:
I moved my Flask app and MySQL into one `docker-compose.yml`. The app starts and crashes at once:

```
sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: (2003, "Can't connect to MySQL server on 'localhost'")
```

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: mysql://root:secret@localhost:3306/app
  db:
    image: mysql:8
```

I already have `depends_on`, so the database should be up first. What am I missing?

answers.body:
There are two problems here.

### 1. The host name

Compose puts every service on a shared network and gives each one a DNS name equal to its service name. From `web`, the database is `db`, not `localhost`:

```
DATABASE_URL: mysql://root:secret@db:3306/app
```

### 2. depends_on does not wait for "ready"

`depends_on` only waits for the `db` container to *start*. MySQL needs a few more seconds before it accepts connections. Add a healthcheck and wait for it:

```yaml
  web:
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: mysql:8
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mysqladmin", "ping", "-h", "localhost"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
```

Note that `localhost` is correct *inside* the healthcheck, because the healthcheck runs inside the `db` container.

comments.author: perezj
comments.text: `condition` only controls startup order. If the database restarts later, the app still needs to retry the connection itself.

answers.body:
Add a link from `web` to `db`:

```yaml
  web:
    links:
      - db
```

comments.author: d.okafor
comments.text: Not needed. Services in one compose file already reach each other by name. It also does not fix the `localhost` in the URL, which is the actual problem.

threads.title: EF Core: Failed to connect to 127.0.0.1:5432 only when running in a container

question.body:
My ASP.NET Core 7 API works with `dotnet run`. In Docker I get:

```
Npgsql.NpgsqlException: Failed to connect to 127.0.0.1:5432
 ---> System.Net.Sockets.SocketException: Connection refused
```

`appsettings.Development.json`:

```json
{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "Default": "Host=localhost;Port=5432;Database=orders;Username=app;Password=app"
  }
}
```

I changed `Host` to my machine's IP address, rebuilt the image, and still get the same error with 127.0.0.1. How?

comments.author: m.verhoef
comments.text: Which environment does the container run in? Without `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` set, ASP.NET Core runs as Production, so `appsettings.Development.json` is never loaded. You edited a file the container does not read.

comments.author: m.verhoef
comments.text: You can override the setting without touching any file: `-e ConnectionStrings__Default="Host=..."`. A double underscore maps to the `:` in the config key.

comments.author: user4471902
comments.text: @m.verhoef that explains why my change did nothing. Still don't know which host to use though.

threads.title: What does localhost mean inside a Docker container?

question.body: If a process inside a container connects to `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`, where does that traffic go? To the container, or to the machine that runs Docker? And how do I reach a service on the host from inside a container?

answers.body:
To the container.

By default every container gets its own **network namespace**: its own interfaces, its own routing table and its own loopback device. `127.0.0.1` inside the container is that container's loopback. It never leaves the container.

Publishing a port (`-p 8080:80`) only works in the other direction: traffic from the host *into* the container.

To reach something outside the container, use an address that exists in the container's network:

- **Another container:** put both on one user-defined network (Compose does this for you) and use the container or service name.
- **The host:** `host.docker.internal` on Docker Desktop. On Linux, map it yourself with `host-gateway`, or use the bridge gateway address (often `172.17.0.1`, check with `docker network inspect bridge`).
- **Share the host's network:** `--network host`. The container then has no network isolation at all, and on Docker Desktop it does not behave the same way as on Linux.

Whichever you pick, the service you connect to must listen on an interface that address can reach. A service bound to `127.0.0.1` on the host is not reachable from a container, even with the right host name.

comments.author: c.ramos
comments.text: The last paragraph should be at the top. Half the duplicates of this question are a database bound to 127.0.0.1.

answers.body:
On Linux with the default bridge network you can find the host from inside the container:

```
ip route | awk '/default/ { print $3 }'
```

That is the gateway address, which is the host.

comments.author: ilya.p
comments.text: The gateway is different on user-defined networks, so do not hard-code what this prints. `host-gateway` is cleaner.

answers.body: Use `0.0.0.0` instead of `localhost` in your connection string. `0.0.0.0` means all interfaces, so it will find the host.

comments.author: b.lindqvist
comments.text: `0.0.0.0` is something a *server* binds to. As a destination, Linux treats it as the local machine, which inside a container is the container. You end up exactly where `localhost` took you.

threads.title: From inside a Docker container on Mac, how do I connect to the host?

question.body: I have a service running on my Mac on port 8000. From a container, `curl localhost:8000` fails. In Docker Toolbox I used the VM's IP address. What is the right way with Docker for Mac?

answers.body:
Docker for Mac provides a special DNS name for this:

```
curl http://docker.for.mac.localhost:8000
```

comments.author: hgreene
comments.text: This name is deprecated. Use `host.docker.internal`, which also works on Docker Desktop for Windows.

comments.author: s.ito
comments.text: Can someone edit the accepted answer? People still copy this.

answers.body:
Use `host.docker.internal`. It replaced the older `docker.for.mac.*` names:

```
curl http://host.docker.internal:8000
```

This name is meant for development on Docker Desktop. Do not rely on it in production.
